subject: science
passage: Ice worms, thin dark relatives of the earthworm only a few centimeters long, live inside glaciers in Alaska and the Pacific Northwest. By day they stay beneath the surface of the ice, but around dusk they rise by the millions to graze on algae growing on the glacier, retreating again before the sun warms the surface. Their bodies are adjusted to the cold so completely that they have little tolerance for anything else. At temperatures a few degrees above freezing an ice worm becomes sluggish, and if it is warmed much further its tissues break down and it dies. Researchers must keep them chilled even during the short trip from glacier to laboratory, and warming glaciers may threaten the worms as surely as the loss of the ice itself.
stem: According to the text, what happens to an ice worm if it is warmed well above the freezing point?

choices.A: Its tissues break down and it dies.
choices.B: It stops feeding on algae and lives on stored energy.
choices.C: It becomes more active, like most other animals.
choices.D: It burrows deeper into the glacier until the surface cools.

explanation.why: The text states the effect of warming directly: a few degrees above freezing the worm "becomes sluggish, and if it is warmed much further its tissues break down and it dies." The correct choice restates this.
explanation.A: Correct. The text says that with further warming "its tissues break down and it dies."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never mentions stored energy or a pause in feeding.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the text: warming makes the worm "sluggish," not more active.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The worms retreat below the surface on a daily schedule, before the sun warms the ice; the text does not say a warmed worm can escape by burrowing.
